blocks.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Th e Second quarterly National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for FY 2024/25 covers 1st July to 31st December 2024. Th e report has been prepared to comply with Article 228(6) of the Constitution and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016, which require the Controller of Budget to submit quarterly budget implementation reports for the National and County governments to Parliament.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Th is is the second budget under the fourth Medium-Term Plan (MTP) (2023-2027) of the Kenya Vision 2030 and is being implemented under the Bottom-up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA) framework. Under this framework, the government aims to achieve economic turnaround and inclusive growth by increasing investments in at least five sectors that significantly impact the economy and household welfare. Th ese sectors include Agricultural Transformation, Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSME), Housing and Settlement, Healthcare, Digital Superhighway, and Creative Industry. Th e agenda also focuses on increasing employment, equitable distribution of income, and social security while expanding the tax revenue base and increasing foreign exchange earnings.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Th e National Government's original gross budget for FY 2024/25 was Kshs.4.49 trillion, revised to Kshs.4.37 trillion in Supplementary Budget I, compared to Kshs.4.34 trillion for FY 2023/24. Th e revised gross budget comprises Kshs.641 billion for ministerial development expenditure, which was 15 per cent of the revised gross national budget and 29 per cent of the revised gross ministerial budget of Kshs.2.23 trillion. Recurrent allocation comprised ministerial allocation of Kshs.1.59 trillion (36 per cent of the revised gross national budget) and Consolidated Fund Services (CFS) at Kshs.2.14 trillion (49 per cent of the revised gross national budget).
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: During the reporting period, receipts into the Consolidated Fund amounted to Kshs.1.74 trillion, representing 41 per cent of the revised estimates of Kshs.4.21 trillion, compared to the Kshs.1.44 trillion (34 per cent) received in a similar period in FY 2023/24. Th e total exchequer issues from the Consolidated Fund to MDAs, CFS, and the County Governments amounted to Kshs.1.71 trillion, representing 41 per cent of the revised net estimates of Kshs.4.21 trillion, compared to Kshs.1.44 trillion recorded in a similar period in FY 2023/24. Th e exchequer issues comprised Kshs.121.82 billion (37 per cent) for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs.654.54 billion (50 per cent) for ministerial recurrent expenditure, Kshs.738.09 billion (35 per cent) to CFS and Kshs.191.62 billion (47 per cent) to County governments as Equitable sharable revenue. County government exchequer issues from the national government include Kshs.30.83 billion for June 2024 arrears and Kshs.160.79 billion for the months July, August, September, October and November 2024.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Th e national government's total expenditure for the first six months amounted to Kshs.1.33 trillion, representing 30 per cent of the national government's revised gross estimates of Kshs.4.37 trillion compared to Kshs.1.64 trillion (36 per cent) recorded in a similar FY 2022/23 period. Th is expenditure comprises of ministerial development expenditure of Kshs.200.21 billion (with an absorption rate of 31 per cent), recurrent ministerial expenditure at Kshs.810.57 billion (absorption rate of 51 per cent) and CFS expenditure at Kshs.316.15 billion (an absorption rate of 15 per cent).
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Expenditure categories with the highest development spending included Capital Transfers by the MDAs in subsidies, grants, or direct transfers to Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) at Kshs.153.07 billion, representing 76 per cent of the gross development spending. Other major development expenditures were
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: the Construction and Civil Works at Kshs.21.93 billion and the Purchase of Specialised Plant, Equipment and Machinery at Kshs.4.74 billion, representing 11 per cent and 2 per cent, respectively, of the gross development expenditure.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: A review of the recurrent expenditure shows that Kshs.304.57 billion. was spent on Compensation to Employees, representing 38 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure by MDAs and 18 per cent of the revenue collected, which is in line with the requirement in PFM Regulations 26(1) of 2015 that ministerial expenditure should not exceed 35 per cent of the national government's equitable share of the revenue raised nationally. Total Current transfers to other government institutions were Kshs.329.22 billion and subsidies Kshs.64.60 billion, representing 41 per cent and 8 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure, respectively. Other expenses with significant expenditure were Kshs.9.56 billion for travel, Kshs. 8.52 billion for security operations, Kshs.8.19 billion for school examinations invigilation, and Kshs.6.87 billion for specialised suppliers.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: During the period under review, some key issues were identified as hampering effective budget implementation. Th ey include underperformance in ordinary revenues and Appropriation-in-Aid, Low absorption of development expenditure, discrepancies between MDAs spending and actual delivery of services, and huge stock of public debt that exceeded the statutory limit thus contravening Section 50 (2) of the PFMA 2012. Th e Controller of Budget also identified slow-paced implementation of equalization fund with 2nd policy projects worth 10.33 billion yet to be funded and policy 1 pending bills relating to the national government still outstanding.  Finally, delays in the implementation of planned development projects was yet another hindrance to enhanced budget execution characterized by many projects overstretching their target completion dates.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: To address the challenges, the Controller of Budget recommends that the government institute strategies to improve revenue generation to ensure that planned activities are funded. Th e government should also implement measures to address challenges facing the implementation of development programmes' and equalization fund and ensure seamless funding to MDAs as per the cashflow projections and approved plans.  Further, prioritize regular audits of public debt procurement and debt utilization, reduction of budget deficit financing through fiscal consolidation and operationalize Section 50(8) of the Public Finance Management Act 2012 by creating a Sinking Fund for loan redemption. Th e government should also fast-track settling of pending bills for policy I projects under Equalization Fund and implementation of the marginalized policy 2 through the timely release of funds to MDAs.  In addition, the MDAs should monitor their planned activities and reallocate the budget for items they cannot fully absorb.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Finally, the Controller of Budget urges MDAs to continuously monitor their budget implementation and ensure strict adherence to results based allocation of resources to enhance service delivery.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: 1.  INTRODUCTION
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: T his report fulfils the requirements of Article 228(6) of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, by presenting progress on the national government's budget implementation in the first six months of FY 2024/2025.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Th e report is presented in Seven chapters. Th e first chapter is the introduction. Th e second chapter presents the status of receipts and exchequer issues in the period under review. It presents revenue estimates and actual receipts into the Consolidated Fund, net exchequer issues to MDAs disaggregated to ministerial development and recurrent vote, Consolidated Fund Services (CFS), and equitable shareable revenue to the forty-seven counties.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Th e third chapter presents the overall budget performance of the national government. Th is includes performance under the Consolidated Fund Services (CFS), MDAs expenditure by economic classification and the position of the pending bill as of 31 December 2024. Th e CFS comprises the public debt disaggregated into external and domestic, pensions and gratuities, salaries, allowances to constitutional office holders and miscellaneous services.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Th e fourth chapter presents the budget performance of the eighty-one MDAs grouped into ten Sectors. Th e ten sectors include (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure, and Information Communications Technology, (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources, (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs, (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order, (vii) Health, (viii) National Security, (ix) Public Administration and International Relations, (x) Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation sector. It presents the MDAs' performance by programmes and sub-programmes and budget absorption.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: In the analysis of budget performance by MDAs, the budget is viewed in gross and net estimates. Th e gross budget comprises Appropriations-in-aid and government grants representing the total vote allocation. Net estimates represent the proportion of the budget to be funded by the government through the exchequer. In the report, the term revised budget refers to Supplementary Budget Estimates I. In examining the funding of planned activities by the government, exchequer issues are expressed as a percentage of the revised net estimates, while the overall budget performance and expenditure are expressed as a percentage of the gross budget, referred to as absorption.   By the end of the first six months of FY 2024/25, the absorption was expected to be 50 per cent of the annual budget.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Chapter Five presents the key issues the Controller of Budget identified as hindering effective budget implementation and provides recommendations to address them. Chapter Six concludes the report.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Annexes support the chapters. Annex I presents major Foreign Currencies Movement, Annex II shows Capital transfer to SAGAs, Annex III details the MDAs' Recurrent Performance by Economic Classification, Annex IV shows Current Transfer, Annex V and VI show MDAs' and State Corporations/State Owned Enterprises/ SAGAs Pending Bills as of 31st December 2024 respectively, Annex VII presents the MDAs' Development Expenditure; Annex VIII details the Recurrent Expenditure, Annex IX, X and XI shows ministerial development and recurrent expenditure per sector and total expenditure per sector respectively.

blocks.text: 2.1.  Introduction
heading_path: 2.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is chapter presents the receipts into the Consolidated Fund and funds released by the National Treasury in the first six months of FY 2024/2025. Th e funds released went towards funding Consolidated Fund Services, ministerial development expenditure, recurrent expenditure, and transfers to the forty-seven counties.
heading_path: 2.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: 2.1.1  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund
heading_path: 2.1.1  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: Th e Consolidated Fund is established under Article 206(1) of the Constitution of Kenya and refers to the account into which all money raised or received by or on behalf of the national government is paid. It excludes monies reasonably exempted by an Act of Parliament and payable into other public funds established for a specific purpose or is retained by the State organ that received it to defray its expenses. Notably, at the beginning of FY 2023/24, the government directed that all money collected by all National Government entities as a fee on services offered be deposited into the e-citizen account, Pay bill number 222222.
heading_path: 2.1.1  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: To finance the budget, the government, through the National Treasury, targeted to raise funds from various revenue sources. Th e sources include Tax Revenue (Kshs.2.48 trillion), Non-Tax Revenue (Kshs.156.35 billion), Domestic borrowing (Kshs.978.30 billion - comprising of net domestic borrowing of Kshs.408.41 billion and internal debt redemption/roll-over of Kshs.569.89 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.593.50 billion) and other Domestic financing (Kshs.4.69 billion). Th e Government also targeted to raise Kshs.573.52 billion from Appropriations in Aid (A-I-A) comprising Kshs.283.65 billion recurrent A-I-A and Kshs.289.87 billion development A-I-A.
heading_path: 2.1.1  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: 2.7.  Exchequer Issues Under Article 223 of the Constitution
heading_path: 2.7.  Exchequer Issues Under Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: Article 223 of the Constitution allows the national government to access additional funding during the budget implementation by spending money that has not been appropriated if the amount appropriated for any purpose under the Appropriation Act is insufficient or a need for unbudgeted expenditure arises for which no amount has been appropriated, or money has been withdrawn from the Contingencies Fund.
heading_path: 2.7.  Exchequer Issues Under Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: In the first six months of FY 2024/2025 exchequer issues pursuant to Article 223 of the Constitution of Kenya was Kshs.16.95 billion, comprising of Kshs.12.80 billion for development expenditure and Kshs.4.15 billion for recurrent expenditure, representing less than 1 per cent (0.04) of the revised gross estimates, compared to 0.07 per cent (Kshs.3.29 billion), issued in a similar period of FY2023/2024. Th is was within the Constitutional threshold of ten per cent of the sum appropriated by Parliament in any particular financial year (Kshs.4.37 trillion for FY 2024/25).

blocks.text: 2.8.  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund
heading_path: 2.8.  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund

blocks.text: Th e Equalisation Fund is established under Article 204 (1) of the Constitution of Kenya, which requires that half a per cent (0.5 per cent) of all the revenue collected by the National government each year, calculated based on the most recent audited revenue received, as approved by the National Assembly, to be paid into the Fund. Article 204(2) of the Constitution provides that the National Government shall use the Equalisation Fund only to provide essential services, including Water, Roads, Health Facilities, and Electricity to marginalised areas to the extent necessary to bring the quality of those services in those areas to the level generally enjoyed by the rest of the nation, so far as is possible.

blocks.text: During the first half of FY 2024/2025, the Controller of Budget authorized 11 requests amounting to Kshs.1.22 billion from the Equalization Fund. heading_path: 3. OVERALL BUDGET PERFORMANCE

blocks.text: 3.1.  Introduction
heading_path: 3.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is chapter presents an overview of the National Government budget implementation in the first six months of FY 2024/25. It also presents the budget performance of the Consolidated Fund Services (which is classified as recurrent expenditure), which contains information on Public debt, Pensions and gratuities, Salaries and Allowances to Constitutional officeholders and Miscellaneous services. Th e chapter further disaggregates expenditure for MDAs under major economic items for the development and recurrent votes, respectively. Th e recurrent vote comprises ministerial allocation and CFS votes. In addition, it presents the status of pending bills as of 31 December 2024.

blocks.text: 3.2.  FY 2024/2025 Overall Budget
heading_path: 3.2.  FY 2024/2025 Overall Budget

blocks.text: Th e approved gross budget for the FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.4.49 trillion, revised to Kshs.4.37 trillion in Supplementary Estimates I, presenting 4 per cent growth compared to Kshs.4.54 trillion in FY 2023/2024. Th is comprised of Kshs.641.00 billion for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs.1.59 trillion for ministerial recurrent expenditures, Kshs.2.14 trillion for CFS. Th is is a decline compared to Kshs.783.22 billion for ministerial development and Kshs.1.68 trillion for ministerial recurrent allocated in the FY 2023/2024. However, CFS allocation increased compared to Kshs.2.08 trillion allocated in FY 2023/2024.
heading_path: 3.2.  FY 2024/2025 Overall Budget

blocks.text: Th e  government targeted to finance the budget through revenue at Kshs.2.64 trillion (including Appropriations-in-Aid) and a deficit financing of Kshs.1.57 trillion (to be funded by Domestic Borrowing, External Loans and Grants at Kshs.978.30 billion and Kshs.593.50 billion, respectively). Th e Domestic Borrowing of Kshs.978.30 billion is comprised of Net Domestic Borrowing of Kshs.408.41 billion and Internal Debt Redemptions of Kshs.569.89 billion. blocks.text: 3.5.  Overdra ft Facility
heading_path: 3.5.  Overdra ft Facility

blocks.text: Th e overdra ft facility is a way of short-term borrowing by the Government to cover temporary cash shortfalls. It is repayable within twelve months. Kenya's Government overdra ft is administered through the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK). It is restricted to a maximum of five percent of the most recently audited revenues and is expected to be paid off by the end of the financial year as specified in Section 15 (3) of the PFM Act.
heading_path: 3.5.  Overdra ft Facility

blocks.text: In the period under review, the overdra ft limit stood at Kshs.97.05 billion and was charged at an average interest rate of 12.3 per cent per annum on the amount outstanding at the end of each month. In the first six months of FY 2024/2025, the total charge on the overdra ft facility was Kshs.3.48 billion, as shown in Table 3.5.

blocks.text: 3.9.1  Introduction
heading_path: 3.9.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is section presents an analysis of the MDAs' expenditure by economic classification for the first six months of FY 2024/2025 of both development and recurrent expenditure. Th e development expenditure is disaggregated into major economic items, which include: Capital Transfers to SAGAs, Civil Works and Construction of Residential and Non-Residential Buildings, Refurbishment of Buildings/infrastructure, Purchase of Specialized Plant, Equipment, and Machinery, and Pre-Feasibility studies.  Conversely, the major economic items for recurrent expenditure are: Compensation to Employees, Operations and Maintenance (O&M), and Current Transfer to SAGAs. O&M is further disaggregated into the major expenditure items which include: Travelling, Printing, and Advertising, Rentals and Rates for Non-Residential Buildings, Training, Hospitality, Maintenance Expenses for motor vehicles, and other assets.

blocks.text: 4. BUDGET PERFORMANCE BY SECTOR
heading_path: 4. BUDGET PERFORMANCE BY SECTOR

blocks.text: 4.1.   Introduction
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: MDAs are classified into ten sectors according to the United Nations Classification of Functions of Government, designed to support fiscal analysis by breaking down Government Fiscal Statistics for comparability. Th e chapter presents the performance of MDAs by sector in the first six months of FY 2024/2025. It provides budget allocations per sector detailing specific MDAs' exchequer issues, expenditures, and absorption on the budget. Th e chapter also presents the performance of MDAs' programmes and sub-programmes and spending on development projects in the first six months of FY 2024/2025.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: Sector performance is presented in alphabetical order as follows; (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT), (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources (EWNR) (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) (vii) Health (viii) National Security (ix) Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation (SPCR) Sectors.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: In FY 2024/2025, the Education Sector was allocated Kshs.628.58 billion, recording the highest budget allocation, attributed to its broad mandate, including primary schools, secondary schools, special education, tertiary education, university education, examinations and curriculum development, and reforms in the education sector. Conversely, the General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector received Kshs.61.42 billion, representing the lowest budgetary allocation.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: 4.2.  Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development Sector
heading_path: 4.2.  Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development Sector

blocks.text: 4.2.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.2.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Agriculture is a devolved function under the fourth schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. It is a critical sector in the economic pillar of the Kenya Vision 2030. Th e ARUD Sector comprises five sub-sectors, namely: Th e State Department for Lands and Physical Planning; the State Department for Livestock Development; the State Department for the Blue Economy and Fisheries; the State Department for Crop Development and the National Land Commission (NLC) together with affiliated Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) and Training Institutions.
heading_path: 4.2.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector is a significant player in the delivery of national development agendas, namely, Kenya Vision 2030, the government plan -the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (2022-27), the Sustainable Development Goals, and the Agricultural Sector Transformation and Growth Strategy among other national and international policies and obligations. During the MTEF period 2024/25-2026/27, the Sector has planned to implement programmes to facilitate food and nutrition security, agro-processing, employment creation, and utilisation of the blue economy .
heading_path: 4.2.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector
heading_path: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector

blocks.text: Th e  budgetary allocation to ARUD in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.82.08 billion, which was revised to Kshs. 73.93 billion in Supplementary Budget I, compared to the Kshs. 98.09 billion allocated in the previous financial year of 2023/24. Th is amount represents 2 percent of the gross national budget of Kshs. 4.37 trillion and 3 percent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs. 2.23 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs. 44.57 billion (60 percent) for development activities and Kshs. 29.36 billion (40 percent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Crop Development received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 42.04 billion (57 percent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for the National Land Commission had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 1.78 billion (2 percent of the ARUD Sector allocation).
heading_path: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector

blocks.text: Th e high allocation to the State Department for Crop Development was due to its Vital role in Agricultural Policy and Research Management, National Food Policy, Strategic Food Reserves, Crop Development, Phytosanitary Services, International Compliance, Agricultural Farmers' Training, and Agricultural Land Resource Inventory management.

blocks.text: 4.4.  Education Sector
heading_path: 4.4.  Education Sector

blocks.text: 4.4.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e  Education Sector comprises four MDAs: Th e  State  Department for Vocational and Technical Training, the State Department for Higher Education and Research, the State Department for Basic Education and the Teachers Service Commission (TSC) and their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector envisions attaining ' Quality and inclusive education, training and research for sustainable development '  in  Kenya. Th e  Sector's  strategic  objectives  include  enhancing access, equity, quality and relevance in education, training and research; establishing, maintaining and managing professional teaching and learning services for all early learning centres, primary, secondary and tertiary institutions; enhancing development ca-
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: pacities for Science Technology and Innovations; enhance mechanisms for dissemination and commercialisation of research findings; improve data quality and sharing in education, training, research and labour market; promote vibrant industry - institutional linkages in the area of skilling for employability; and integrate ICT in Education, Training and Research for management, teaching and learning at all levels.
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: It is worth noting that the ongoing education transitions from the 8-4-4 to the 2-6-6-3 system require substantial infrastructure, equipment and human capital in FY 2024/25 and the medium-term 2024/25 to 2026/27.
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.4.2  Budget Performance for Education Sector
heading_path: 4.4.2  Budget Performance for Education Sector

blocks.text: Th e budgetary allocation to Education in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs 656.55 billion, which was revised to Kshs.627.77 billion in Supplementary Budget I, compared to the Kshs. 689.40 billion allocated in FY 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 14 percent of the revised gross national budget of Kshs.4.37 trillion and 28 percent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs. 2.23 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs. 21.09 billion (3 percent) for development activities and Kshs. 606.68 billion (97 percent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e Teachers Service Commission received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 347.89 billion (55 percent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Vocational and Technical Training (TVET) had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 28.21 billion (5 percent of the Education Sector allocation).

blocks.text: Th e high allocation to the Teachers Service Commission is attributed to its vital role in Teacher Resource Management programme. Figure 4.3 shows the budgetary allocation trends of the Education Sector for the period FY 2020/2021 to FY 2024/2025.

blocks.text: 4.4.18 Th e Teachers Service Commission
heading_path: 4.4.18 Th e Teachers Service Commission

blocks.text: Th e Teachers Service Commission is mandated to formulate policies to regulate the teaching profession and guide teacher management functions, thus ensuring compliance with the teaching standards prescribed from time to time, facilitating teachers' career progression and professional development and monitoring their conduct and performance during curriculum implementation.  TSC registers trained teachers and recruits, employs, and assigns teachers employed by the commission. It also exercises disciplinary controls over registered teachers, terminate the employment of the teachers, review the standards of education and training of persons entering the teaching service, reviews the demand for and supply of teachers, and advises the national government on matters relating to the teaching profession.

blocks.text: 4.5.  Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT) Sector
heading_path: 4.5.  Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT) Sector

blocks.text: 4.5.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is Sector consists of nine MDAs: Th e State Department for Roads, Transport, Shipping and Maritime Affairs, Housing and Urban Development, Public Works, Information Communications Technology and Digital Economy, Broadcasting and Telecommunications, Energy, and Petroleum.
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e EIICT sector aims to provide sustainable infrastructure development, a vibrant shipping and maritime industry, universal access to Information Communications Technology (ICT), Transport and built environment services, and accessible, affordable, quality and competitive energy and petroleum products.
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e EI&ICT Sector plays a vital role as an enabler of the country's socio-economic development. It is a crucial sector in realising Vision 2030 and the BETA Agenda.
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.5.2  Budget Performance for EIICT Sector
heading_path: 4.5.2  Budget Performance for EIICT Sector

blocks.text: Th e budgetary allocation to EIICT in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.476.04 billion, which was revised to Kshs. 444.29 billion in Supplementary Budget I, compared to the Kshs. 534.36 billion allocated in the previous financial year of 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 10 percent of the gross national budget of Kshs. 4.37 trillion and 20 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs. 2.23 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs. 302.26 billion (68 percent) for development activities and Kshs. 142.03 billion (32 percent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Roads received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 191.98 billion (43 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Shipping and Maritime Affairs had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 2.97 billion (less than 1 percent of the EIICT Sector allocation).

blocks.text: 4.5.8 Th e State Department for Transport
heading_path: 4.5.8 Th e State Department for Transport

blocks.text: Th e State Department of Transport promotes the management of transport policy; manage rail transport and infrastructure; fast track identified northern and LAPPSET transport corridor projects; oversight and co-ordinate northern corridor transport and implement Lamu South Sudan Ethiopia transit (LAPSSET) programmes; civil aviation management and training; registration and insurance of motor vehicles; motor vehicles inspection; national transport safety; national road safety management; national roads transport policy; axle load control policy and standards; develop and maintain air strips; and oversee the establish an integrated, efficient, effective and sustainable urban public transport system within the Nairobi metropolitan area. Th e mandate is carried out by the State Department of Transport and its agencies, Th e Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA), Kenya Airports Authority (KAA), Kenya Railways Corporation (KRC), LAPSSET Corridor Development Authority (LCDA), Kenya Ports Authority (KPA), National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) and Th e Nairobi Metropolitan Area Transport Authority (NaMATA)

blocks.text: 4.5.13 Th e State Department for Shipping and  Maritime Affairs
heading_path: 4.5.13 Th e State Department for Shipping and  Maritime Affairs

blocks.text: Th e State Department for Shipping and  Maritime Affairs promotes the maritime and shipping industry; manages maritime transport; ship registration; marine cargo insurance; human resource development, management and research in support of Kenya's shipping industry; establish an effective admiralty jurisdiction; develop a central data and information centre; co-ordinate maritime spatial planning and integrated coastal zone management; protect and regulate marine ecosystems; develop national capacity for Kenya's maritime sector;

blocks.text: 4.6.  Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources Sector
heading_path: 4.6.  Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources Sector

blocks.text: 4.6.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources (EPWNR) Sector comprises six MDAs: State Departments for Environment & Climate Change; Forestry; Water and Sanitation; Irrigation; Wildlife; and Mining. Th e sector has several autonomous and semi-autonomous government agencies. In addition, the Sector has the following entities: Th e National Environment Complaint Committee, the National Environment Tribunal, the Hydrologists Registration Board, and the Wildlife Clubs of Kenya.
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e goal of the Sector is ensuring sustainable development in a clean and secure environment with various objectives, including enhancing climate change resilience and low carbon emission, improving utilisation of land through irrigation and land reclamation, and promoting equitable and sustainable use of wildlife resources.
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector plays a pivotal role in securing, stewarding, and sustaining the environment, Kenya's natural capital, water provision, and generating foreign exchange for the country. Th e Sector promotes socio-economic development to realise the Kenya Vision 2030 and BETA Agenda.
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.6.2  Budget Performance for EPWNR Sector
heading_path: 4.6.2  Budget Performance for EPWNR Sector

blocks.text: Th e  budget allocation to EPWNR in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.109.73 billion, which was revised to Kshs.101.20 billion in Supplementary Budget I, compared to the Kshs.120.56 billion allocated in a similar period FY 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 2 per cent of the revised gross national budget of Kshs.4.37 trillion and 5 percent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.23 trillion. Th e allocation comprises Kshs.69.04 billion (68 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.32.15 billion (32 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Water and Sanitation received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.49.84 billion (49 per
heading_path: 4.6.2  Budget Performance for EPWNR Sector

blocks.text: cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Mining had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.994.87 million (less than 1 per cent of the EPWNR Sector allocation).

blocks.text: 4.7.  General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector
heading_path: 4.7.  General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector

blocks.text: 4.7.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) sector consists of eight MDAs, namely the State Departments for Trade; Arid and Semi-arid Lands (ASALs) and Regional Development; Cooperatives; Industry; Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development; Investment Promotion; East African Community; and Tourism together with their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.
heading_path: 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e main objectives of the Sector over the MTEF period are to transform Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), promote and sustain tourism, promote industrial development investments, enhance trade and ease of doing business, promote growth and development of cooperatives and the MSMEs Sector, promote regional integration, and promote equitable and sustainable ASAL and regional development.
heading_path: 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.7.2  Budget Performance for GECA Sector
heading_path: 4.7.2  Budget Performance for GECA Sector

blocks.text: Th e budgetary allocation to GECA in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.57.67 billion, which was revised to Kshs. 45.63 billion in Supplementary Budget I, compared to the Kshs. 61.42 billion allocated in the Financial Year of 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 1 percent of the gross national budget of Kshs. 4.37 trillion and 2 percent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs. 2.23 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs. 15.76 billion (35 percent) for development activities and Kshs. 29.87 billion (65 percent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Tourism received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 10.32 billion (23 percent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for East African Community had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 0.57 billion (1 percent of the GECA Sector allocation).

heading_path: 4.7.8 Th e State Department for the ASALs and Regional Development

blocks.text: Th e State Department for the ASALs and Regional Development promotes Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Policy; Coordination of Planning, and Development for Arid and Semi-Arid Lands; Implementation of Special Programmes for the Development of Arid and Semi-Arid Areas; Implementation of Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Programmes; Coordinating Research for sustainable Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Resource Management, Development and Livelihoods; Promotion of Livestock Development, Marketing and Value addition of Resources within Arid and Semi-Arid Areas; Enhancing Livelihood Resilience of Pastoral and Agro Pastoral Communities; Coordinating Responses Against Drought and Desertification; Special Programmes; Food Relief Management and Humanitarian Emergency Response; Peace Building and Conflict Management within Arid and Semi-Arid Area; Management and Promotion of Integrated Cross-border Activities in Identified ASAL Counties;  Regional  Development Policy Implementation, Oversight and Management; Coordination of Regional Development Authorities; and Projects in Response to Displacement Impacts. blocks.text: 4.8.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector
heading_path: 4.8.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector

blocks.text: 4.8.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector consists of sixteen MDAs, which include the State Department for Correctional Services; the State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services; the National Police Service; the State Department for Internal Security and National Administration; the State Law Office; the Judiciary; the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC); the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP); the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP); the Witness Protection Agency (WPA); the  Kenya  National  Commission  on  Human  Rights  (KNHCR);  the  Independent  Electoral  and  Boundaries Commission (IEBC); the Judicial Service Commission (JSC); the National Police Service Commission (NPSC); the National Gender and Equality Commission (NGEC); and the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), as well as SAGAs and tribunals each with specific functions and mandates.
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector creates a conducive environment for the country's economic, social, and political development necessary for fulfilling the objectives of the Kenya Vision 2030. It comprises institutions with linkages to peace- and security-building, interpretation of the law, correctional services, immigration and population management, legal advisory services to government agencies, representation of the national government in civil proceedings and matters before foreign courts and tribunals, and dispensation of justice. Further, the Sector promotes good governance and integrity and spearheads the fight against corruption, public prosecutions, registration and regulation of political parties, protection of witnesses, protection and promotion of human rights, delimitation of electoral boundaries and management of the electoral process, promotion of gender equality, the inclusion of marginalised groups and communities.
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector is also responsible for developing and implementing citizenship and refugee management and immigration services, regulating the gaming industry, providing population management, eradicating drugs and substance abuse, conducting crime research, printing government documents, and overseeing policing.
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.8.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector
heading_path: 4.8.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector

blocks.text: Th e budgetary allocation to GJLO in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.246.42 billion, which was revised to Kshs.231.06 billion in Supplementary Budget I, compared to the Kshs.259.49 billion allocated in the previous financial year of 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 5 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.37 trillion and 10 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.23 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs.5.88 billion (2 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.225.18 billion (98 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for National Police Service received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.108.68 billion (47 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for National Gender and Equality Commission had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.0.41 billion (less than 1 per cent of the GJLO Sector allocation).
heading_path: 4.8.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector

blocks.text: Th e high allocation to the State Department for National Police Service was due to providing security to the government's critical infrastructure and other related activities. Figure 4.11 shows the budgetary allocation trends of the GJLO Sector from FY 2020/2021 to FY 2024/25.

Th is amount comprised Kshs.4.69 billion for development expenditure, representing147 per cent of development net estimates, and Kshs.115.32 billion for recurrent activities, representing 52 per cent of recurrent net estimates.

Conversely, the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions received the lowest exchequer issues at 26 per cent. Th e State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services recorded the highest proportion of recurrent exchequer issues to recurrent net estimates of 70 per cent. heading_path: 4.8.23 Th e State Law Office

heading_path: 4.8.38 Th e Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions

blocks.text: 4.9.  Health Sector
heading_path: 4.9.  Health Sector

blocks.text: 4.9.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.9.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Health is largely a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. Th e health sector is responsible for providing and coordinating health policy formulation, ensuring quality service delivery, and regulating health care at the national level. Th e sector comprises two MDAs: Th e State Department for Medical Services and the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards. Th e Sector delivers services through several SAGAs and entities, including the Kenyatta National Hospital, Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, Kenya Medical Research Institute, Kenya Medical Supplies Authority, Kenya Medical Training College, National Syndemic Disease Control Council, Kenyatta University Teaching, Referral and Research Hospital, National Cancer Institute of Kenya and the Kenya Nuclear Regulatory Authority.
heading_path: 4.9.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector envisions 'a healthy, productive and globally competitive nation ' achieved through strategic objectives under equity, efficiency, and people-centred principles with a multi-sectoral approach as outlined in the Kenya Health Policy (2014-2030). Th e Health Sector implements its strategic objectives through eight budgetary programmes, four under the State Department for Medical Services and four under the State Department for Public Health and Professionals.
heading_path: 4.9.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.9.2  Budget Performance for Health Sector
heading_path: 4.9.2  Budget Performance for Health Sector

blocks.text: Th e budgetary allocation to Health in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.127.17 billion, revised to Kshs.118.86 billion in Supplementary Budget I, compared to the Kshs.134.76 billion allocated in FY 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 3 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.37 trillion and 5 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.23 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs.32.03 billion (27 percent) for development activities and Kshs. 86.83 billion (73 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Medical Services received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 91.98 billion (77 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards was allocated Kshs.26.87 billion (23 per cent of the Health Sector allocation).
heading_path: 4.9.2  Budget Performance for Health Sector

blocks.text: Th e high allocation to the State Department for Medical Services was due to high budget allocation in the National Referral Services sub programme. Figure 4.13 shows the budgetary allocation trends of the Health Sector for the period FY 2020/2021 to FY 2024/2025.

blocks.text: 4.9.8 Th e State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards
heading_path: 4.9.8 Th e State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards

blocks.text: Th e State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards promotes quality healthcare services are guaranteed through the provision of policies on healthcare, standards, human resource development, and public health standards and sanitation management. It is also tasked with strategic leadership and support to all health professional bodies, development of a framework to ensure the sharing of professional experiences and embedding in future clinical practice. Th e mandate is carried out by the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards and its agencies; the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentist Council (KMPDC), Kenya Medical Training College (KMTC), Kenya Health Professions Oversight Authority (KHPOA), Kenya National Public Health Institute (KNPHI) and Kenya Medical Laboratory Technicians and Technologists Board (KMLTTB).

blocks.text: 4.10.  National Security Sector
heading_path: 4.10.  National Security Sector

blocks.text: 4.10.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e National Security sector comprise the Ministry of Defence and the National Intelligence Service (NIS). Th e sector's mandate is to ensure the country's security against any threats emanating from within or outside the Kenyan borders, defend the country, and support the civil powers in maintaining peace and order.
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.10.2  Budget Performance for National Security Sector
heading_path: 4.10.2  Budget Performance for National Security Sector

blocks.text: Th e  original  budget  for  the  National  Security  sector  in  FY  2024/2025  was  Kshs.219.44  billion,  revised  to Kshs.219.30 billion in Supplementary I, representing 5.0 per cent of the revised gross national budget, compared to Kshs.211.63 billion allocated in the FY 2023/2024. Th e  allocation  comprised Kshs.1.53 billion for development expenditure (1 per cent of the sector's budget) and Kshs.217.77 billion for recurrent expenditure (99 per cent of the sector's allocation). Th e Ministry of Defence was allocated Kshs.172.95 billion (79 per cent of the sector's allocation), while NIS received Kshs.46.35 billion (21 per cent of the sector's allocation). Th e growth in the budget allocation for the National Security sector is attributed to increased funding requirements for military modernisation, enhanced territorial defence capabilities, and strengthened intelligence-gathering operations.

blocks.text: 4.10.3 Th e Ministry of Defence
heading_path: 4.10.3 Th e Ministry of Defence

blocks.text: Th e Ministry of Defence encompasses the Kenya Army, Kenya Air Force, Kenya Navy, Defence Forces Constabulary and Civilian Staff. It envisions itself as a premier, credible, and mission-capable force grounded in professionalism. Its primary mandate is to defend and protect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Kenya, while its secondary mandate includes assisting and cooperating with other authorities during emergencies or disasters and restoring peace in any part of Kenya affected by unrest or instability as directed. Th e Ministry is committed to defending and protecting the people and property of the Republic of Kenya against external threats and supporting civil authority as per the law.

blocks.text: 4.11.  Public Administration and International Relations Sector
heading_path: 4.11.  Public Administration and International Relations Sector

blocks.text: 4.11.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) sector consists of twenty-three MDAs, namely Th e Executive Office of the President, Office of the Deputy President, Office of the Prime Cabinet Secretary, State  Department for Parliamentary Affairs, State Department for Performance and Delivery Management; State Department for Cabinet Affairs; State House; State Department for Devolution; State Department of Economic Planning; State Department for Foreign Affairs; State Department for Diaspora Affairs; Th e National Treasury; State Department for Public Service; Parliamentary Service Commission; National Assembly; Parliamentary Joint Services; Senate; Th e Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA); Public Service Commission; Salaries and Remuneration Commission; Th e Auditor General ; Th e Controller of Budget and Th e Commission on Administrative Justice (CAJ) together with affiliated SAGAs and entities.
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e  Sector  provides  national  leadership,  oversight,  and  policy  direction  towards  realising  the  country's  development agenda. It promotes prudent public finance management and accountability in the Public Sector, coordinates national and sectoral development planning, and oversees an efficient and effective Public Service. It also coordinates Kenya's foreign policy and diaspora affairs, wage bill management, development of a sound legislative and regulatory framework, and enforces administrative justice and the right to information.
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e  sector  has  prioritised  programmes  and  projects  aligned  with  the  Post-COVID-19  Economic  Recovery Stimulus Programme (PC-ERS), the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda, and the Fourth Medium Term Plan of Kenya Vision 2030. Priority was also accorded to ongoing interventions supporting the 'Big Four' agenda and the newly established institutions.
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

Th is amount represents 7 percent of the gross national budget of Kshs. 4.37 trillion and 14 percent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs. 2.23 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs. 125.34 billion (42 percent) for development activities and Kshs. 176.44 billion (59 percent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e National Treasury received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 119.23 billion (40 percent of the Sector's budget),

blocks.text: 4.12.  Social Protection, Culture and Recreation Sector
heading_path: 4.12.  Social Protection, Culture and Recreation Sector

blocks.text: 4.12.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.12.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation (SPCR) Sector comprises six MDAs: the State Departments for Youth Affairs and the Arts, Sports, Culture and Heritage, Labour and Skills Development, Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs, and Gender and Affirmative Action.
heading_path: 4.12.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e strategic roles played by the Sector in the country's transformation and socio-economic development include Promoting and supporting youth empowerment and development; strengthening youth mainstreaming in  all  sectors;  spearheading  the  management  of  youth  policy  and  legislations;  promoting  engagement  with youth for national development; promotion of sustainable employment, harmonious industrial relations, and productive workforce; promotion of gender equity and equality; empowerment of communities and vulnerable groups, safeguarding children's rights; and advancement of diverse cultures, arts and sports to enhance cohesiveness and Kenya's regional and international competitiveness
heading_path: 4.12.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.12.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector
heading_path: 4.12.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector

blocks.text: Th e budgetary allocation to SPCR in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.72.07 billion, revised to Kshs.68.94 billion in Supplementary Budget I, compared to the Kshs.72.85 billion allocated in the previous financial year of 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 2 percent of the revised gross national budget of Kshs. 4.37 trillion and 3 percent of the MDAs' revised budget of Kshs.2.23 trillion. Th e allocation comprises Kshs.23.66 billion (34 percent) for development activities and Kshs.45.28 billion (66 percent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.35.17 billion (51 percent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Culture and Heritage had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.2.83 billion (4 percent of the SPCR Sector allocation).

blocks.text: Th e non-financial performance analysis indicated that despite significant spending on some projects by the State Department for Labour and Skills Development, there was a considerable lag in completion rates. blocks.text: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS
heading_path: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS

blocks.text: Th e Controller of Budget identified critical issues discussed while overseeing budget implementation in the first six months of FY 2024/25.
heading_path: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS

blocks.text: 5.1.  Receipts into the Consolidated Fund
heading_path: 5.1.  Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: Observation: In the first six months of FY 2024/25, receipts into the Consolidated Fund amounted to Kshs.1.75 trillion, representing 40 per cent of the revised annual target of Kshs.4.21 trillion against the estimated 50 per cent threshold on a linear basis. Th is implies that 10 per cent of the annual value of budgeted activities were not implemented. Th e shortfall in revenue was attributed to the withdrawal of the Finance Bill 2024, affecting some of the targeted revenue sources.
heading_path: 5.1.  Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: Further analysis shows that actual revenue receipts are mainly funded from ordinary tax revenue, which constitutes 62 per cent of total receipts revenue, followed by domestic borrowing at 27 per cent. Receipts from non-tax revenue, external loans, and grants underperformed, given that the three categories did not achieve the estimated 50 per cent threshold as of 31 December 2024.
heading_path: 5.1.  Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: Recommendations: Th e Controller of Budget is cognisant of the tight fiscal constraints the government has been facing. Th e shortfall in revenue collection has severe consequences for budget implementation. It may delay the financing of various government programmes and necessitate a supplementary budget to align with the revenue pattern. It calls for further stringent measures to improve ordinary revenue and Appropriations-In-Aid by Ministries, Departments and Agencies and County governments to supplement the defraying of expenditure and reduce overreliance on funding from the exchequer.
heading_path: 5.1.  Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: 5.2.  Low Absorption of Development Budget
heading_path: 5.2.  Low Absorption of Development Budget

blocks.text: Observation: In the first six months of FY 2024/25, the national government's total expenditure was Kshs.1.76 trillion, representing 40 per cent of the revised gross budget. Th is comprised ministerial development expenditure of Kshs.200.35 billion (absorption rate of 31 per cent), ministerial recurrent expenditure of Kshs.810.57 billion (absorption rate of 50 per cent), and Consolidated Fund Services, Kshs.751.20 billion (absorption rate of 35 per cent).
heading_path: 5.2.  Low Absorption of Development Budget

blocks.text: Th e low absorption of development is attributed to a shortfall in receipts into the Consolidated Fund and the need to prioritise funding of public debt, which is a first charge to the Consolidated Fund, and other non-discretionary recurrent expenditure such as compensation to employees. Further analysis of project implementation shows that some multi-year projects were not funded in the period under review and others with negligible expenditure indicating a delay in project implementation.
heading_path: 5.2.  Low Absorption of Development Budget

blocks.text: Recommendation: Development  projects  and  programmes  must  be  monitored. Th e  National  Treasury  should release funds to the MDAs per the cash flow projections and approved plans for seamless implementation to ensure projects are completed in a timely manner. Th is will curb the accumulation of pending bills and additional costs related to delays in project completion on both the demand and supply sides.
heading_path: 5.2.  Low Absorption of Development Budget

blocks.text: 5.3.  Slow-paced Implementation of the Equalization Fund
heading_path: 5.3.  Slow-paced Implementation of the Equalization Fund

blocks.text: Observation: Article 204 of the Constitution requires one-half per cent (0.5 per cent) of all the revenue collected by the national government each year calculated based on the most recent audited statement ( Auditor General's ) of revenue received as approved by the National Assembly. As of 31 December 2024, the National Treasury had disbursed Kshs.1.03 billion only and is yet to provide and disburse the balance of funds owed to the Equalization Fund to implement the 2 nd policy projects worth Kshs.10.33 billion. Notably, the Fund has yet to clear pending bills at the national government level for Policy 1 consideration.
heading_path: 5.3.  Slow-paced Implementation of the Equalization Fund

blocks.text: Recommendations: Th e slow pace of implementing the Equalization Fund development budget is a fiscal concern given that the Equalization Fund had a significant balance of over Kshs.10 billion as of the end of the first half of FY 2024/25. Th e Controller of Budget recommends fast-tracking the settlement of pending billings related to the first Policy and the implementation of Second Policy.
heading_path: 5.3.  Slow-paced Implementation of the Equalization Fund

blocks.text: 5.4.  Public debt Stock exceeding the Authorised Limit
heading_path: 5.4.  Public debt Stock exceeding the Authorised Limit

blocks.text: Section 50 (2) of the PFMA 2012 states that the National Government may borrow money under this Act or any other legislation and shall not exceed the limit set by Parliament. Th e Public debt ceiling was set at 55 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product by Parliament. Th e Budget Review Outlook Paper 2024 indicates that Kenya's GDP was Kshs.16.11 trillion as at 30 th June 2024.
heading_path: 5.4.  Public debt Stock exceeding the Authorised Limit

blocks.text: Observation: As of 31 December 2024, the public debt stock was Kshs.10.93 trillion (68 of the GDP), with Kshs.5.06 trillion owed to external lenders (46 per cent) and Kshs.5.87 trillion owed to domestic lenders (54 per cent). The public debt stock increased by 3 per cent from Kshs.10.58 trillion as of 30 June 2024 to Kshs10.93 trillion as of 31 December 2024. External debt declined by 0.2 per cent due to the appreciation of the Kenya Shilling against major world currencies, while domestic debt recorded 8 per cent growth attributable to increased borrowing in the domestic market. The 2025 Medium Term Debt Management Strategy (MTDS)
heading_path: 5.4.  Public debt Stock exceeding the Authorised Limit

blocks.text: indicates that total nominal public debt as a percentage of GDP in Kenya has been declining, decreasing from 72 per cent in 2022 to 66 per cent in June 2024. The public debt therefore remains above the authorised public debt limit.
heading_path: 5.4.  Public debt Stock exceeding the Authorised Limit

blocks.text: Recommendations: Th e Controller of Budget recommends regular audits of public debt procurement and debt utilization to ensure transparency and reduction of budget deficit financing through fiscal consolidation. Further, the National Treasury should operationalize Section 50(8) of the Public Finance Management Act 2012 by creating a Sinking Fund for loan redemption. Th is dedicated fund will ensure systematic savings for loan repayment, reduce reliance on new debt for refinancing, and enhance fiscal discipline in debt management.
heading_path: 5.4.  Public debt Stock exceeding the Authorised Limit

blocks.text: 5.5.  Delayed Completion of Development Projects
heading_path: 5.5.  Delayed Completion of Development Projects

blocks.text: Observation  An  analysis  of  the  development  projects'  implementation  by  Ministries,  Departments  and Agencies of the National Government revealed general delay in projects implementation . For instance, Kenya Affordable Housing Finance and Registration of Community Land - Isiolo South projects did not record any expenditure in the first half of FY 2024/25 while Geo-referencing land parcels project recorded completion rate of 19 per cent despite the project commencing in July 2013. Also, six  (6)  development projects implemented by the State Department for Transport had over-stretched their target completion dates. Th e projects include Development of Nairobi Railway City (completion date of 30 th June 2023), Construction of 2.8Km new MGR link from Mombasa SGR Terminus - Miritini MGR station and railway bridge across Makupa causeway (completion date of 30 th June 2024), Revitalization of Gilgil - Nyahururu MGR Branch line (completion date
heading_path: 5.5.  Delayed Completion of Development Projects

blocks.text: of 30 th June 2024), Revitalization of Kisumu - Butere MGR Branch line (completion date of 30 th June 2024), Construction of Access Road to Suswa SGR Station  and to Maai Mahiu SGR Station (completion date of 30 th June 2024), and Revitalisation of Leseru- Kitale MGR Branch (completion date of 30 th June 2024). Further, four (4) development projects implemented by the State Department for Information, Communication Technology & Digital Economy namely; Maintenance and Rehabilitation of NOFBI Phase II Cable (completion date of 31/12/18), Maintenance and Rehabilitation of NOFBI Phase II Expansion (completion date of 31/12/20), Connectivity to Leather Industrial Park- Kenaine (completion date of 01/12/22), and Construction of KAIST at Konza Technopolis (completion date of 31/12/24) were still on-going as at 31 st December, 2024 thus faced with the completion date overrun.
heading_path: 5.5.  Delayed Completion of Development Projects

blocks.text: Recommendation: Measures should be taken to address the projects implementation challenges by the MDAs with a view to fast track the completion of all the affected multi-year projects whose completion rate are behind the target timelines.
heading_path: 5.5.  Delayed Completion of Development Projects

blocks.text: 5.5.1  Inconsistencies between MDAs' spending and non-financial performance
heading_path: 5.5.1  Inconsistencies between MDAs' spending and non-financial performance

blocks.text: Observation: Budget execution entails delivering services by undertaking expenditures within regulatory controls of the law by line Ministries, spending Departments and and Agencies. In the first half of FY 2024/2025 we noted instances of significant spending by MDAs without correspending outputs or depressed service delivery. For example, the State Department for Public Works recorded total expenditure of Kshs.1.34 billion but no outputs in the first six months of FY 2024/25, casting doubts on how the funds already spent were put to use. Besides, Non-financial performance analysis the State Department for East African Community indicated that no changes in actual outputs from service delivery have occurred since the end of first quarter (first three months) of FY 2024/25, which appear impractical . In addition, the State Department for Immigration and Citizens Services   spent Kshs.12.66 billion (ab sorption rate of 89 per cent ) on programmes and sub-programmes. Expenditure on E-citizens Services and immigration services sub-programmes under Migration and Citizen Services Management Programme exceeded the budgetary allocation by 329 per cent and 9 per cent respectively. However, actual outputs from delivery of services were below 35 per cent for all the p rogrammes and sub-programmes it implemented in the period under review.
heading_path: 5.5.1  Inconsistencies between MDAs' spending and non-financial performance

blocks.text: Recommendation: Th e  Controller  of  Budget  recommends continuous monitoring of budget implementatation and strict adherence to results based allocations of resources to spur service delivery.
heading_path: 5.5.1  Inconsistencies between MDAs' spending and non-financial performance

blocks.text: 6. CONCLUSION
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Th e National Government Budget Implementation Report provides financial and non-financial information on budget performance for the first six months of FY 2024/25, covering 1st July to 31st December 2024. It presents revenue outturn, debt financing, expenditure performance, budget absorption and discusses key issues affecting overall budget execution.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: During the period, the national government budget performance remained resilient despite the interruptions at the start of the financial year following the withdrawal of Finance Bill 2024, which affected revenue generation and budget implementation. Th e overall budget absorption rate was 40 percent of the revised gross budget, which is below the target of 50 per cent in the first six months of FY 2024/25.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Total receipts into the Consolidated Fund were Kshs. 1.74 trillion, representing 41 per cent of the revised annual target. Th e Controller of Budget approved the withdrawal of Kshs.1.71 trillion from the Consolidated Fund, representing 41 per cent of the revised net estimates, implying 9 per cent of targeted activities were not funded based on the target of 50 per cent in the first six months. Th e exchequer issues comprised Kshs.129.82 billion for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs.654.54 billion for ministerial recurrent expenditure, Kshs.738.09 billion for Consolidated Fund Services and Kshs.191.62 billion as disbursements of revenues raised nationally to County Governments. Th e Ministerial recurrent expenditure recorded the highest proportion of exchequer issues to revised net estimates at 50 per cent due to limited fiscal space and the pressure to maintain service delivery levels. Consolidated fund services recorded the least proportion of exchequer issues to revised net estimates at 35 per cent.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Gross expenditure for the National Government was Kshs.1.76 trillion, recording an absorption rate of 40 per cent. Th is  comprised ministerial development expenditure at Kshs.200.35 billion (absorption rate of 31 per cent), ministerial recurrent expenditure at Kshs.810.57 billion (absorption rate of 51 per cent), and Consolidated Fund Services at Kshs.751.20 billion (35 per cent). Th e development budget recorded the lowest absorption, implying delayed projects implementation during the period under review.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Th e Controller of Budget lauds the government's milestone in budget implementation despite several challenges that hampered budget implementation. Depressed revenue outturn and huge public debt continue to strain the fiscal space thus negatively affecting the execution of government programmes. Further, rationalisation of the budget to accommodate revenue shortfalls following the withdrawal Finance Bill of 2024 at the beginning of financial year led to further shrinking of the fiscal space and increase in pending bills.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Finally, the low level of budget absorption indicates that some planned activities were not implemented. Respective government entities are encouraged to identify other challenges that delay budget absorption and address them in the subsequent budget implementation period. Programmes with low budget absorption should be fast-tracked to enhance effective service delivery.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION
